reason: I'll start with the muscle fibre, since the current goal is to make it pull and reset.
expectation: I expect the cell to gain muscle-fibre structures, though further parts will be needed for pulling.

effect: The cell is now an elongated muscle fibre with spaces for contractile units, so I can add the pulling machinery.
reaction: The retained cell structures make the transition to a muscle fibre clear.
reason: Sliding filaments fit the fibre's spaces and should help it pull, matching the current goal.
expectation: I expect actin and myosin units to be installed in the fibre; a further signal may be needed for pulling.

alternatives.reason: The triceps belongs on the skeleton, but I want to finish the fibre's pulling machinery first.

effect: The fibre now has ATP-ready filament units, but the actin grip sites remain covered, so a signal appears necessary before pulling.
reaction: The reset myosin head and covered grip sites make the remaining obstacle clear.
reason: The calcium signal is the offered next step for activating the filament units.
expectation: I expect calcium to expose the actin grip sites and allow myosin to pull, though resetting may require another step.

alternatives.reason: Attaching the triceps is also useful, but the fibre's pulling mechanism is still unfinished.

effect: Calcium exposed the grip sites, allowing myosin to pull the filaments past one another; the fibre now needs to become ready again.
reaction: The distinction between the fibre shortening and the filaments sliding without shortening is useful.
reason: The calcium-pumping membranes seem relevant to removing the calcium signal and resetting the fibre.
expectation: I expect the pumps to return calcium to storage so the fibre can relax and become ready again, likely using ATP.

alternatives.reason: The triceps will help build the arm, but the current fibre goal still includes resetting.

effect: ATP-powered pumps return calcium to storage, stopping the pull and readying the fibre; the next goal is to connect opposing muscle pulls to the arm bones.
reaction: It's useful to see that relaxation also requires ATP and that an outside pull lengthens the fibre.
reason: I'll gather the fibre with others as a step toward building a muscle that can pull on the bones.
expectation: I expect a group of muscle fibres, likely needing connective tissue before it can carry a pull to the skeleton.

alternatives.reason: Attaching the triceps also serves the new goal, but I'll build up the other muscle first.

effect: The fibres now form a parallel bundle, with the examined structures identified in one fibre. It still needs a way to transmit its pull.
reaction: The paired poses connect the individual fibre to the larger bundle.
reason: Connective tissue sheaths seem like the next step toward carrying the bundle's pull to bone.
expectation: I expect the bundle to gain connective tissue, though it may still need a tendon or another connection to the skeleton.

alternatives.reason: The triceps also contributes to opposing pulls, but I want to build the fibre bundle further first.

effect: The sheaths gather the fibre bundle into a biceps with tendons, providing attachment points for the skeleton.
reaction: The connection from fibres through connective tissue to tendons is clear; I hadn't expected the bundle to become a named biceps immediately.
reason: I'll attach the biceps to the skeleton to carry its pull into the bones.
expectation: I expect the biceps tendons to attach to the arm skeleton and allow a pull across the elbow; the opposing triceps may still be needed.

alternatives.reason: The triceps also needs attaching, but I'll connect the newly built biceps first.

effect: The biceps now spans the elbow and pulls the forearm upward; the assembly still has an empty extensor slot.
reaction: The two poses make the biceps pull clear, though the extensor label relies on knowing its role.
reason: The triceps is the only offered combination and should supply the opposing pull.
expectation: I expect the triceps to fill the extensor slot and help straighten the elbow; further work may still be needed.

effect: The triceps now provides the opposing pull, straightening the elbow as it shortens. The arm assembly can next receive blood vessels.
reaction: The paired movements clarify how muscles pull in opposite directions rather than push.
reason: Adding limb blood vessels is the only offered combination and may supply the arm's tissues.
expectation: I expect vessels to branch through the arm and supply its muscles, though I don't know whether that completes the goal.

effect: The vessels now branch among the muscle fibres, completing the opposing-pulls goal while leaving their connection to the larger circulation for later.
reaction: The vessel beside the ATP-making machinery connects the arm back to the earlier cell model, though the supply relationship is only suggested.

mostWorthwhile.text: The calcium signal and sliding-filament construction was most worthwhile: the planned poses distinguish a shortening fibre from filaments that slide without shortening, and show ATP's role in the myosin cycle.

leastWorthwhile.text: Gathering the fibres into a bundle felt comparatively routine. The paired poses connect scales, but the result adds less explanation than the surrounding constructions.

surprise.text: I was surprised that adding connective-tissue sheaths immediately produced a named biceps with tendons; the picture explains how the sheaths gather into tendons, but the identification as biceps was abrupt.

arbitrary.text: The extensor slot could be unclear to students unfamiliar with the term. The triceps was the only offered combination, and its straightening role became clear after fitting it.

continue.text: Yes, I would continue out of curiosity about how the arm's vessels connect to the larger circulation. The final illustration plan leaves that connection open.
